chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyih (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, from his uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abi al-Sabah al-Kanani, from Abi Basir, from Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Three are the hardest things for the servants to do: a believer being fair to himself, a man sharing with his brother, and remembering God in every state.
This is that he remembers God, the Exalted, when about to commit a sin, so the remembrance of God stands between him and that sin.
Indeed, those who fear God, when an impulse touches them from Satan, they remember [God], and at once they see clearly.
And this is the saying of God, the Exalted.

key_terms.أَنْصَافُ الْمُؤْمِنِ مِنْ نَفْسِهِ: A believer being fair to himself
key_terms.مَوَاسَاةُ الْمَرْءِ أَخَاهُ: A man sharing with his brother

ai.seo_question: What are the three hardest deeds for believers according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights these three acts as 'hardest' because they require conscious effort against the self's inclinations, particularly the practice of *dhikr* acting as a spiritual brake during the moment of temptation. This specific application of remembrance to prevent sin underscores the Shia emphasis on *muraqabah* (God-consciousness) as a practical mechanism for moral preservation. The narration links the internal state of the believer directly to the Quranic concept of *tadhakkara* (remembrance) as the catalyst for clarity (*mubsiroon*).
